blocks.content: When you see https in your browser, TLS is what the S actually stands for. TLS, Transport Layer Security, is the protocol that secures communication between two parties over a network, and the handshake is the negotiation that happens before either side sends a single byte of real data.
When you open a website over HTTPS, TLS sits between your browser and the server and protects every byte exchanged between them.
1. What TLS Actually Provides
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273704813-523199537.png
blocks.alt: TLS provides three distinct guarantees at once, not just encryption alone

blocks.content: TLS provides three things. Encryption means when you send a password or a credit card number, TLS scrambles it, anyone who intercepts the traffic sees only meaningless characters. Authentication means TLS helps your browser verify the server is genuinely the website you intended to visit, not an imposter. Integrity means TLS detects if anyone tampers with the data while it travels across the network, the data arrives exactly as it was sent, or the tampering is caught.

All three of these guarantees are established once, during the handshake itself, and then apply automatically to every single byte exchanged for the rest of that connection, without the application ever needing to think about encryption directly.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026910-607113277.png
blocks.alt: TLS sits between the transport layer and the application layer, running its own handshake only after TCP has already connected

blocks.content: TLS sits between the transport layer, TCP, and the application layer, HTTP. TCP establishes a connection first, TLS then runs its handshake on top of that connection, and only after that completes does actual HTTP data begin flowing.
2. Before TLS: The TCP Handshake

TLS never runs in isolation, a TCP connection must exist first, established through the three way handshake covered in depth in the OSI Model and TCP vs UDP topics, a client SYN, a server SYN-ACK, and a client ACK, after which both sides know the other is reachable and ready.

Only after TCP is established does TLS even begin. This is exactly why HTTPS carries slightly more latency than plain HTTP, you pay for both the TCP setup and the TLS setup before any real data flows.

TLS 1.3's own reduction from two round trips to one, covered later in this topic, and session resumption together exist specifically to shrink this exact combined cost back down for the overwhelming majority of real connections.
3. The Two Sides of the Handshake
blocks.text: 3. The Two Sides of the Handshake

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273708327-633273589.png
blocks.alt: Each side brings different information into the handshake before secure communication can even be negotiated

blocks.content: The client, a browser, mobile app, or API caller, already knows which TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, generates a random value of its own, and carries a built in list of Certificate Authorities it already trusts. The server holds a TLS certificate, proving its identity, and a private key, used to help establish the secure connection without ever exposing that key itself.

Neither side needs to know anything about the other's own internal setup beforehand, the entire handshake exists precisely to let two parties that have never spoken before agree on everything they need to, safely, in real time.

The handshake is fundamentally how these two sides agree on how to talk, verify each other's identity, and generate a shared encryption key, all without that key ever once being sent directly over the network.
4. Cipher Suites
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273710007-38517524.png
blocks.alt: A cipher suite bundles together exactly how key exchange, encryption, and integrity checking will work for this one connection

blocks.content: A cipher suite is a bundle of algorithms defining exactly how encryption works for one session. The client offers a list of suites it supports, the server picks one from that list. Key exchange decides how the two sides agree on a shared secret without ever transmitting it directly, algorithms like ECDHE handle this. In TLS 1.3, this negotiation was simplified considerably, cipher suites only specify the encryption and hash, key exchange is always ECDHE, giving forward secrecy by default rather than as an optional extra.

A cipher suite's name reads left to right as exactly this bundle, for example naming its key exchange method, its encryption algorithm and key length, and its hashing algorithm in sequence, which is why two suite names that look similar can still differ meaningfully in a single one of those components.
5. The TLS 1.2 Handshake
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273711774-440012080.png
blocks.alt: TLS 1.2 needs two full round trips before any encrypted application data can flow

blocks.content: TLS 1.2 takes two round trips before encrypted data can flow. The client sends a Client Hello carrying its supported versions, cipher suites, and a random value. The server replies with a Server Hello, selecting one version and one cipher suite, along with its own random value, then sends its certificate to prove its identity.

The client verifies that certificate, then generates a Pre-Master Secret, encrypts it with the server's public key, and sends it across, only the server's matching private key can decrypt it. Both sides now independently combine the client random, server random, and pre-master secret into the same session keys, which are never transmitted over the network at all. Both sides exchange a Change Cipher Spec message and an encrypted Finished message, proving the handshake itself was never tampered with, and only then does encrypted application data actually begin.

blocks.title: Where the Keys Actually Come From
blocks.content: The Client Random, Server Random, and Pre-Master Secret combine into a Master Secret, computed independently by both sides. That Master Secret then generates the actual Session Keys used to encrypt and decrypt everything for the rest of the connection.
6. Certificate Verification: How Trust Works
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026911-458426161.png
blocks.alt: A server's certificate is vouched for by an intermediate authority, which is itself vouched for by a root already trusted by your browser

blocks.content: The single most important step in the handshake is the client verifying the server's certificate, this is exactly what prevents connecting to an imposter. Certificates never stand alone, they form a chain. At the top sits the Root CA, an organization like DigiCert or Let's Encrypt already trusted by your operating system and browser. Rather than signing every website's certificate directly, the Root CA signs an Intermediate CA certificate, and that intermediate authority signs the actual website's own certificate.

Your browser verifies the entire chain at once, the server certificate was genuinely signed by the intermediate, the intermediate was genuinely signed by the root, and that root is already in the browser's own trusted list. If every link in that chain checks out, the connection is trusted.
7. How the Client Validates a Certificate
blocks.text: 7. How the Client Validates a Certificate

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027100-219253210.png
blocks.alt: Any single failed check anywhere in this sequence rejects the certificate outright, rather than accepting it with a caveat

blocks.content: ["The domain name in the certificate must match the site actually being visited, a mismatch is rejected immediately","The certificate must not have expired, an expired certificate can no longer be trusted no matter how valid it once was","The chain must lead all the way to a Root CA the browser already trusts, following server certificate to intermediate to root","The certificate must not have been revoked, checked against services like OCSP, since even a technically valid certificate may have been compromised after issuance"]
items: The domain name in the certificate must match the site actually being visited, a mismatch is rejected immediately
The certificate must not have expired, an expired certificate can no longer be trusted no matter how valid it once was
The chain must lead all the way to a Root CA the browser already trusts, following server certificate to intermediate to root
The certificate must not have been revoked, checked against services like OCSP, since even a technically valid certificate may have been compromised after issuance

blocks.content: If every one of these checks passes, the server's identity is confirmed and the handshake continues. If even one fails, the browser shows a certificate warning and terminates the connection outright, this is exactly why an expired certificate blocks the page entirely rather than merely showing a subtle notice.

None of these checks are optional or skippable by the browser on its own, a user can sometimes choose to click through a warning and proceed anyway, but that is a deliberate, explicit override of the check, not the check itself failing to run.
8. The TLS 1.3 Handshake: Faster and Safer
blocks.text: 8. The TLS 1.3 Handshake: Faster and Safer

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273717129-610072867.png
blocks.alt: TLS 1.3 collapses the handshake into a single round trip by having the client send its key share immediately, before the server even asks for it

blocks.content: TLS 1.3, released in 2018, redesigned the handshake from scratch, and the single biggest change is one round trip instead of two. The client sends its Client Hello and, critically, its own key share, its ephemeral public key, immediately in that very first message, a calculated bet that the server supports the same key exchange algorithm, rather than waiting to be asked.

The server responds with its own key share, its certificate, and proof it owns the corresponding private key, all of it already encrypted, unlike TLS 1.2 where these were sent in the clear. The client verifies everything and sends its own Finished message, and secure communication begins having spent only a single round trip, not two.

9. Forward Secrecy: Why It Matters
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273718773-51421394.png
blocks.alt: Without forward secrecy, stealing the server's long term private key years later can retroactively decrypt every session ever recorded

blocks.content: In older TLS using RSA key exchange, the pre-master secret is encrypted directly with the server's long term public key. If an attacker recorded all of your encrypted traffic today and later stole that server's private key, years from now, they could decrypt every one of those old recorded sessions, including the very old ones, all at once.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273720477-25847267.png
blocks.alt: With forward secrecy, a fresh ephemeral key exists only for one session and is gone forever once that session ends

blocks.content: Forward secrecy, via ECDHE, prevents exactly this. A brand new, temporary key pair is generated for every single session, and that ephemeral private key is discarded the instant the session ends. Even if an attacker later steals the server's long term private key, that key was never used to protect the actual session key in the first place, only to prove the server's identity, so old sessions stay genuinely safe.

Stealing a server's long term private key today can expose years of past communication under RSA key exchange. Under ECDHE, it exposes nothing about any past session at all, which is exactly why TLS 1.3 made forward secrecy mandatory and removed RSA key exchange entirely.

The example below simulates exactly this contrast with real, if intentionally small, math. Under ECDHE, the client and server each independently derive the identical shared session key through Diffie-Hellman, using their own ephemeral private values, and once the server's ephemeral private value is gone, an attacker holding only the server's separate, long term key cannot reconstruct that same session key at all. Under RSA-style key exchange, the exact same long term key that was compromised is the one that can decrypt the recorded pre-master secret directly, exposing the old session key completely.

codes.python:
def mod_pow(base, exponent, modulus):
    result = 1
    base = base % modulus
    while exponent > 0:
        if exponent & 1:
            result = (result * base) % modulus
        exponent >>= 1
        base = (base * base) % modulus
    return result


def main():
    p = 23  # small prime, illustrative only, never use tiny numbers like this in real TLS
    g = 5   # generator

    # --- ECDHE-style: forward secrecy ---
    client_private = 6
    server_ephemeral_private = 15  # discarded the instant this session ends

    client_public = mod_pow(g, client_private, p)
    server_ephemeral_public = mod_pow(g, server_ephemeral_private, p)

    client_shared_secret = mod_pow(server_ephemeral_public, client_private, p)
    server_shared_secret = mod_pow(client_public, server_ephemeral_private, p)
    print("ECDHE: client-derived session key =", client_shared_secret)
    print("ECDHE: server-derived session key =", server_shared_secret)
    print("ECDHE: both sides agree =", client_shared_secret == server_shared_secret)

    # Years later, an attacker steals the server's separate, long-term signing key.
    server_long_term_key = 999
    attacker_attempt = mod_pow(client_public, server_long_term_key % (p - 1), p)
    print(f"Attacker using the long-term key gets: {attacker_attempt} "
          f"(matches real session key: {attacker_attempt == client_shared_secret})")

    # --- RSA-style: no forward secrecy ---
    pre_master_secret = 42
    cipher_text = pre_master_secret ^ server_long_term_key  # simple reversible stand-in for "encrypted with the server's key"
    print("RSA-style: pre-master secret sent as ciphertext", cipher_text)

    attacker_recovered_secret = cipher_text ^ server_long_term_key  # same key that was stolen
    print(f"Attacker using the SAME stolen long-term key recovers: {attacker_recovered_secret} "
          f"(matches original pre-master secret: {attacker_recovered_secret == pre_master_secret})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

blocks.content: 10. Session Resumption: Skipping the Full Handshake
blocks.text: 10. Session Resumption: Skipping the Full Handshake

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273722181-599093267.png
blocks.alt: A session ID lets a returning client skip the expensive parts of the handshake, at the cost of the server remembering that session

blocks.content: A full handshake is genuinely expensive. When reconnecting to a server visited before, TLS lets most of it be skipped entirely. On the first connection, after a complete handshake, the server creates a Session ID and stores that session's information in memory. On reconnection, the client sends that same Session ID inside its Client Hello, the server recognizes it, and both sides simply resume the existing session rather than repeating certificate verification and key exchange from scratch.

blocks.title: The Real Limitation
blocks.content: Session IDs require the server to store session state for every single client it has ever talked to recently, which scales poorly once traffic is spread across many different servers behind a load balancer.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027285-795647911.png
blocks.alt: A session ticket is stateless, the client itself carries the encrypted session information, so any server in a fleet can resume it

blocks.content: Session tickets solve exactly that scaling problem. Instead of storing session information in memory, the server encrypts it into a ticket and hands that ticket to the client. On reconnection, the client presents the ticket, and any server capable of decrypting it, even one that never handled the original connection at all, can resume the session immediately. This makes session tickets genuinely stateless, and considerably more scalable across a large, distributed server fleet.

This distinction matters enormously the instant a real deployment sits behind a load balancer spreading traffic across many interchangeable servers, a returning client's second connection has no guarantee of landing on the exact same server as its first, which session IDs alone simply cannot handle gracefully.
11. 0-RTT Resumption in TLS 1.3
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273725428-448038332.png
blocks.alt: TLS 1.3 lets a returning client send real application data in its very first message, before the handshake has even finished, but only safely for repeatable requests

blocks.content: TLS 1.3 goes a step further still. On a reconnection, the client can send actual application data in the very first message, before the handshake formally completes at all, genuinely zero additional round trips for the data itself.

blocks.title: The Real Trade-Off
blocks.content: 0-RTT data is vulnerable to replay attacks, an attacker who captured that first message can resend it, and the server has no way to tell the difference from a genuine repeat request. 0-RTT should only ever be used for safe, idempotent operations, an ordinary GET request, never something like submitting a payment.
12. SNI: Server Name Indication
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027094-668675712.png
blocks.alt: SNI tells the server which of its many hosted certificates to actually present, before the connection is even encrypted

blocks.content: A single server IP can host thousands of completely different websites, each with its own certificate. Without SNI, the server only sees the incoming IP address, with no way to know which of its many certificates to present, and might send the wrong one entirely, triggering a certificate error even for a genuinely valid site.

SNI solves this by having the client include the specific hostname it wants inside the Client Hello itself. The server reads that hostname and immediately sends back the correct, matching certificate. This is exactly what lets many independent HTTPS websites safely share the same IP address, each with its own separate certificate.

Before SNI existed, hosting multiple HTTPS sites on shared infrastructure required a dedicated IP address per certificate, which is exactly why SNI's introduction was such a meaningful, practical unlock for affordable shared HTTPS hosting at scale.

blocks.title: A Real Privacy Gap
blocks.content: SNI is sent in the Client Hello as plain text, even on an otherwise fully encrypted HTTPS connection. This means an observer on the network path can still see which domain you are connecting to, just not anything about the actual data exchanged afterward.
13. What Can Go Wrong

14. The Full Picture: TLS 1.3 End to End
blocks.text: 14. The Full Picture: TLS 1.3 End to End

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273728799-492859.png
blocks.alt: TCP connects, TLS negotiates and verifies, and only then does encrypted application data actually begin flowing

blocks.content: A TCP connection is established through SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. The client sends a Client Hello with its supported version, cipher suites, random value, key share, and SNI. The server responds with a Server Hello, selects the cipher suite, and sends its own key share, letting both sides derive handshake keys immediately. The server sends its certificate and proves ownership of the matching private key, the client verifies the full certificate chain, both sides exchange Finished messages, and from that point forward, every request and response is encrypted using the session keys just derived.
Worked Example

A payments API deliberately disables 0-RTT for its checkout endpoint specifically, since a captured and replayed checkout request could trigger a duplicate charge, but leaves 0-RTT enabled for its read-only product catalog endpoint, where a replayed request simply returns the same catalog data twice, a harmless outcome.

The same team also automates certificate renewal well ahead of each certificate's expiry date, and monitors their own TLS configuration for any cipher suite considered weak, exactly the operational discipline this topic's common failure modes point toward avoiding.

They also deliberately keep session tickets, not session IDs, as their resumption mechanism of choice, specifically because their API runs behind a fleet of many interchangeable servers, and a session ID's server-side memory requirement would tie a returning client to whichever specific server happened to handle its very first connection.
Common Mistakes

["Assuming TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 negotiate identically, and being surprised when a client that only supports very old cipher suites fails to connect to a server that has removed them","Enabling 0-RTT for an endpoint that is not genuinely idempotent, opening the door to replay-based duplicate actions","Treating an expired certificate as a minor inconvenience rather than an outage, since browsers reject the connection entirely rather than merely warning","Forgetting that SNI is sent unencrypted, and assuming HTTPS alone hides which domains a device is connecting to"]
items: Assuming TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 negotiate identically, and being surprised when a client that only supports very old cipher suites fails to connect to a server that has removed them
Enabling 0-RTT for an endpoint that is not genuinely idempotent, opening the door to replay-based duplicate actions
Treating an expired certificate as a minor inconvenience rather than an outage, since browsers reject the connection entirely rather than merely warning
Forgetting that SNI is sent unencrypted, and assuming HTTPS alone hides which domains a device is connecting to

blocks.content: Practice

Use a browser's developer tools to inspect the TLS details of a connection to any HTTPS site you use daily, identify the negotiated TLS version and cipher suite, and note whether the certificate chain includes an intermediate authority before reaching a trusted root.

Then explain, in your own words, why a server that only supports TLS 1.0 and 1.1 would fail to connect with a modern browser, and what specifically about those old versions makes them unsafe to keep supporting today.
Key Takeaway

The TLS handshake is how a client and server agree on encryption settings, verify the server's identity through a certificate chain of trust, and generate shared session keys, all without ever transmitting those keys directly. TLS 1.3 cut this process from two round trips to one by having the client send its key share immediately, and made forward secrecy mandatory, so even a stolen long term key years later reveals nothing about sessions that already ended. Session resumption and 0-RTT both trade a small amount of security nuance for real speed on repeat connections, which is exactly why knowing precisely what each trade-off actually costs matters more than treating TLS as a black box that simply works.

Every one of the mechanisms covered in this topic, cipher suites, certificate chains, forward secrecy, session resumption, exists to answer the exact same underlying question in a slightly different context: how do two parties that have never met establish trust and secrecy together, quickly, without ever exposing the very keys that trust depends on.
